candidates.name: Qt — thread-safe versus reentrant
candidates.reason: Qt's separate term thread-safe for concurrent use of one instance provides a clearer concurrency label than a word that merely describes shared access.
candidates.application_scope: Naming precedent for ThreadSafe or an explicitly qualified concurrent-sharing trait; keep the trait's existing shared-reference contract.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Qt's definition covers class operations generally; Rust's trait should remain specifically about safe concurrent access through shared references, without promising unrestricted mutation or requiring locks.
candidates.date_evidence: Opened Qt 6.12 live documentation; its publication date was not established, and the Qt 4.8 archive attempt failed.

candidates.name: Boost — shared ownership versus thread safety
candidates.reason: Boost's separate shared-ownership terminology and thread-safety contract show why sharing alone should not name a concurrent-safety guarantee.
candidates.application_scope: Terminology and documentation structure: describe aliasing or ownership separately from operations safe across threads.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: A shared_ptr is an owning handle rather than a Rust borrow; its documented handle operations do not make every access to its pointee safe.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened official versioned Boost 1.55.0 documentation explicitly states that this release is from 2013, before 2014-08-05.

candidates.reason: Concurrent Ruby describes mutable abstractions as thread-safe, providing a precedent for naming concurrent safety without suggesting immutability.
candidates.application_scope: Trait documentation and naming examples that permit safely synchronized interior mutation.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Ruby's library guarantees are per abstraction and do not automatically cover referenced mutable payloads; this is a vocabulary precedent, not a transferable Rust trait definition.
candidates.date_evidence: Opened the live README; no historical version establishing these statements by the cutoff was verified.

candidates.reason: Clang separates shared or exclusive access capabilities from thread-safety obligations, illustrating how access vocabulary and concurrency guarantees can occupy different naming layers.
candidates.application_scope: Documentation vocabulary and avoidance of mechanism-specific trait names such as Locked or Guarded.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: These are annotation-based access requirements, not a universal marker for values safely shared through a Rust reference; the mechanism must not replace the trait's existing semantic property.

raw_response:
C22 — catalogue baseline B

Five naming precedents were verified. The useful distinction is between access that can have aliases and the additional guarantee that such access remains safe across concurrent threads. Any rename must retain the latter guarantee exactly.

1. Qt — thread-safe versus reentrant
https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/threads-reentrancy.html
Qt distinguishes safe concurrent use of one instance from concurrent use of separate instances. This supports an explicit concurrency name such as ThreadSafe. Its class-wide terminology is broader than the Rust trait, so retain the narrower shared-reference contract.
Discovery: https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp
Date: unknown; the live Qt 6.12 page was verified, but the attempted older archive was inaccessible.

2. Boost — shared ownership versus thread safety
https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/libs/smart_ptr/shared_ptr.htm
Boost documents shared ownership and concurrency rules separately. This supports reserving shared for the access or ownership relationship while giving concurrency safety a separate label. An owning handle is not a borrow, and handle safety does not establish universal pointee safety.
Discovery: https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp
Date: pre-decision; the official versioned page identifies Boost 1.55 as a 2013 release.

3. Concurrent Ruby — thread safety separate from mutability
https://github.com/ruby-concurrency/concurrent-ruby
The library uses thread-safe terminology for mutable abstractions. This helps explain that a concurrency-safety trait can permit interior mutation. Its guarantees are abstraction-specific and do not make arbitrary referenced mutable payloads safe.
Discovery: https://github.com/markets/awesome-ruby/blob/master/README.md
Date: unknown; only the live README was verified.

4. Clang Thread Safety Analysis — access capabilities and safety contracts
https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThreadSafetyAnalysis.html
Clang's shared/exclusive capability vocabulary is distinct from its thread-safety obligations. This illustrates separate naming layers for access permissions and concurrency protection. Its annotations specify access conditions; they are not equivalent to the Rust marker trait.
Discovery: https://github.com/kassane/awesome-concurrency/blob/main/README.md
Date: unknown; historical verification attempts failed.

5. Pony reference capabilities — aliasing, read-only access, and actor sharing
https://tutorial.ponylang.io/reference-capabilities/reference-capabilities.html
Pony separates aliasable mutable references, read-only views, immutable values, and isolated transfer. In particular, its box view may refer to data another local alias can mutate. This is a useful comparison, but Pony's actor-sharing rules must not replace the Rust trait's semantics.
Discovery: https://github.com/kassane/awesome-concurrency/blob/main/README.md
Date: unknown; no dated tutorial version was verified. An auxiliary PDF's general Rust discussion was conservatively excluded from clean evidence.

Translation to the naming problem

ThreadSafe has an observed naming precedent. ConcurrentShareable is an inferred descriptive alternative, not a discovered established trait name. Either would need a precise definition: safe concurrent access to a value through shared references. Ordinary shared access alone does not establish the trait; immutability, ownership transfer, absence of aliases, and use of a particular synchronization mechanism must not become substitute definitions.

These are terminology precedents, not evidence that a rename was adopted or proved useful. The run used six searches and twenty-two explicit page-open attempts: seventeen succeeded and five failed. It returned five candidates. Only the Boost source was established as pre-decision; the other candidate evidence remains date-unknown.
